What more cases buy: inferential targets for reproduction-number estimates and what cross-sectional dispersion diagnostics measure

[Author names and affiliations to be added before submission]
5 November 2026

1 Introduction

Reproduction numbers summarise transmission under specified conditions and are routinely estimated from surveillance counts [1, 2]. Renewal methods relate incidence to past infectiousness through a generation-interval distribution, and the width of their credible intervals shrinks as the number of cases grows [3, 4]. Work on low incidence, reporting noise and timely detection has made the limits of period-specific inference explicit [5–7], and temporal aggregation and reporting delays separate the reproduction number of the transmission process from the apparent reproduction number of an observed series [8–10].

Precision guidance for renewal estimators is often stated in cases. Under a gamma prior with shape a0, the posterior coefficient of variation of the renewal estimator of Cori et al. [3] is (a0+IW)−1/2, where IW is the number of cases in the window, so it is a function of the window count alone. Their Web Appendix 3 uses this relation to suggest that estimation start once at least 12 cases have accrued since the first case, which gives a posterior coefficient of variation of about 0.3; this heuristic is one of three criteria they give for the start of estimation. The coefficient measures counting error for the average transmission level over the window. The estimate is also often read as the transmission level now or as a typical level for the population. For those targets, variation between periods is an additional error component that more cases do not remove. A count-based criterion is therefore complete for one target and incomplete for the other two.

The variance structure behind this distinction is classical. Variance-component models split the variance of a unit-level estimate into a within-unit sampling term and a between-unit term [11, 12]. Random-effects meta-analysis estimates the between-study component on top of within-study error [13], and small-area estimation and empirical-Bayes disease mapping weight each direct estimate against a common mean according to the ratio of the two terms [14–16]. Funnel plots for institutional comparison draw control limits from the counting term and, when units differ beyond chance, add an overdispersion component; in the additive random-effects form the variance of a unit indicator based on n events is σ2/n+τ2 [17, 18]. The affine dispersion model used below has exactly this form. Population ecology makes the same split between demographic and environmental stochasticity [19, 20], as do stochastic epidemic models [21, 22]. In each setting the count at which the two terms are equal is where a shrinkage estimator places half its weight on the direct estimate.

Several results used below are standard and are cited where they are applied. The mean squared error decompositions follow from the law of total variance [11, 23]. The efficiency of the count-to-scale ratio for a Poisson mean is the Cramér–Rao bound [24], the delta-method expansion of a ratio estimator is textbook material [23], and the square-root allocation of surveillance effort is Neyman allocation [12]. Offspring overdispersion follows Lloyd-Smith et al. [25], and its estimation from small samples Lloyd-Smith [26]. A variance that scales as a power of the mean is Taylor’s law [27]. The distinction between the realised quantity of a finite population and the parameter of the process that generated it follows Graubard and Korn [28]; the case reproduction number of Wallinga and Teunis [29] is a realised quantity of this kind. Constant under-reporting cancels from ratio estimators of the reproduction number, whereas reporting that changes over time does not [2, 3]. Choosing the estimation window to balance counting noise against changes in transmission is the aim of adaptive windowing [30], and hierarchical renewal models pool an observation layer across regions [31].

The paper is a synthesis of these results for period-specific reproduction numbers, together with a cross-sectional diagnostic and an application under a written analysis plan. Section 2 sets out three inferential targets, derives their exact mean squared errors in a branching model with negative binomial offspring and binomial reporting, and gives the correction required when the denominator is the previous observed count. Section 3 shows that, when the reporting probability fluctuates between periods, single-period second moments of the counts cannot separate reporting volatility from transmission variation. Section 4 defines the diagnostic, an affine regression of the squared relative deviation of an apparent reproduction number on inverse count, maps its intercept and slope to the quantities of the model, and states the analysis plan. Section 5 applies the plan to 1,748 state-weeks of US influenza hospital admissions. The primary question is narrow: whether a count-independent component of dispersion remains after counting noise is allowed for. The secondary questions are how large it is at the counts actually observed, whether the affine form describes it, and whether it is common to jurisdictions of different size.

The question matters because routine hospital surveillance does not observe the variables of a branching experiment. Admissions follow infection after a delay, aggregate heterogeneous populations and are recorded on a calendar schedule, and their count scale is an outcome of the epidemic. Reporting probabilities may change for all infections in the same period [32, 33], and separating process from observation variation in time series is a known difficulty [34, 35]. The cross-sectional spread of growth-rate or reproduction-number estimates has been read as variation in transmission or behaviour between places and periods without subtracting the part of that spread that depends on case counts [36, 37], although per-unit standard errors make the subtraction possible [38]. The diagnostic performs that subtraction. Its intercept bounds what additional cases can buy, but by the result of Section 3 it does not separate transmission from reporting, and the analysis reads it as reflecting both rather than as an estimate of their sum. Section 6 discusses real-time use, reporting that depends on transmission and the choice of generation interval. Proofs, extensions and a known-truth simulation audit on the real design are in the appendices.

2 Model and inferential targets

2.1 A branching experiment with a known observation scale

Consider one generation of transmission with n≥1 primary infections. Conditional on the reproduction number Rt>0, the offspring counts of primary cases are independent negative binomial variables [25]:

Xi,t∣Rt∼NB(k,k/(k+Rt)),E(Xi,t∣Rt)=Rt,Var(Xi,t∣Rt)=Rt+Rt2k,(1)

where k>0 controls individual heterogeneity. Each secondary infection is independently reported with probability ρ∈(0,1]. Summation over primary cases and binomial thinning give the law of the reported count:

Ct∣n,Rt∼NB(nk,k/(k+ρRt)),E(Ct∣n,Rt)=ρnRt,Var(Ct∣n,Rt)=ρnRt+ρ2nRt2k.(2)

Define m=ρn and R̂t=Ct/m. The scale m is the expected reported count at Rt=1, not the realised count Ct.

The baseline assumptions are fixed, known ρ with independent reporting (H1); conditionally independent offspring as in Eq. (1) (H2); fixed, known k (H3); and a fixed or exogenous n that does not depend on transmission (H4). Write E(Rt)=R¯>0 and Var(Rt)=vR<∞. Across periods, counts are independent given the whole transmission trajectory, each with conditional law (2). These are repeated branching experiments; they do not assert that naturally evolving incidence is exogenous. Dividing by an assumed ρ0≠ρ gives conditional mean (ρ/ρ0)Rt, a multiplicative bias that more cases do not remove.

The conditional counting variance combines offspring randomness and omission. Conditioning on the total number of secondary infections splits it into (Rt+Rt2/k)/n and (1−ρ)Rt/(ρn). The term linear in Rt is therefore not purely reporting noise; it remains under complete reporting.

2.2 Current values, realised means and process means

For the current target, E(R̂t∣Rt)=Rt and Var(R̂t∣Rt)=(Rt+ρRt2/k)/m, which attains the Cramér–Rao bound for estimators unbiased for every Rt under this likelihood (Appendix A.1).

Proposition 1 (One period, two targets). Under H1–H4, let A=R¯+ρ(R¯2+vR)/k. The two risks of R̂t are:

E[(R̂t−Rt)2]=Am,V(m):=E[(R̂t−R¯)2]=vR+Am.(3)

Among estimators based on this period’s count that are conditionally unbiased for Rt, R̂t minimises both risks.

The proof (Appendix A.2) squares the error decomposition:

R̂t−R¯=(R̂t−Rt)+(Rt−R¯).(4)

The two terms on the right are uncorrelated. Between-period transmission variation is part of the signal for the current value and sampling error for the process mean, which is a mean under a stated stationary law and not automatically a seasonal average of a nonstationary epidemic.

For vR>0 define the crossover scale m×=A/vR, the expected count at which the two terms of V(m) are equal. Its meaning is the one it has in small-area estimation [14]. The best linear predictor of Rt from R̂t under the stated moments takes the form:

R¯+γ(m)(R̂t−R¯),γ(m)=vRvR+A/m=mm+m×,(5)

so m× is the count at which shrinkage gives the direct estimate half its weight. Doubling m through n at fixed ρ, k and transmission law reduces process-mean risk by the fraction 1/[2(1+m/m×)], which is one quarter at m=m× and less beyond it. Changing ρ changes A as well as m. The scale m× describes the selected estimator and target; it does not mark a point where information stops accumulating.

Corollary 1 (A fixed set of observed periods). Under H1–H4 and conditional independence of counts given R1:T, let R¯T denote the mean of R1,…,RT and R̂¯T the mean of R̂1,…,R̂T. If the Rt share common marginal moments, the two mean targets have risks:

E[(R̂¯T−R¯T)2]=ATm,E[(R̂¯T−R¯)2]=BT+ATm,BT=Var(R¯T).(6)

In Eq. (6), BT=vR/T for independent, identically distributed Rt. For a stationary process with Cov(Rt,Rt+h)=vRϕ|h|, |ϕ|<1, BT=vRS(ϕ,T)/T2 exactly, where the window sum is:

S(ϕ,T)=T+2∑h=1T−1(T−h)ϕh=T(1+ϕ)1−ϕ−2ϕ(1−ϕT)(1−ϕ)2.(7)

The realised-mean identity needs only conditionally independent counting errors, not independent transmission levels. More cases in the same periods remove its counting error, while process-mean risk tends to BT; only more periods reduce BT, at a rate set by their dependence. Positive persistence reduces the gain from adjacent periods. Spatial averaging behaves analogously. For J units with transmission variance vR and mean pairwise correlation c¯, the averaged transmission level has the variance:

Var(J−1∑j=1JRj,t)=vR[c¯+(1−c¯)/J].(8)

Figure 1 plots these risks, with known-truth Monte Carlo checks, and Table 2 collects them.

2.3 An observed denominator

Surveillance ratios divide by an observed count rather than by a known scale. Let the denominator be the reported count of the primary generation, Mt∼Bin(n,ρ), independent of the offspring given n, and let R̃t=Ct/Mt. Because Mt=m(1+ut) with Var(ut)=(1−ρ)/m, a delta expansion (Appendix A.5) gives the approximate risk:

E[(R̃t−Rt)2]≈A+(1−ρ)(R¯2+vR)m,(9)

so the crossover scale moves to m×+(1−ρ)(R¯2+vR)/vR. With R¯=1.15, vR=0.04, k=0.35 and ρ=0.25 (A=2.1232) it rises from 53.1 to 78.6. Monte Carlo with 400,000 draws per scale (Table 3) puts the observed-denominator error at 1.59, 1.51 and 1.49 times A/m for m=50, 200 and 1000, close to the delta value of 1.48. At m=10 the ratio is 2.42 and the delta form understates the error, because small denominators inflate the ratio. The ratio estimator is undefined when Mt=0; such draws are excluded and their share is reported in Table 3, where it is zero to the precision shown at every scale considered. At m=10 the Monte Carlo error is 0.5145 with standard error 0.0048. A continuity-corrected ratio, (Ct+0.5)/(Mt+0.5), lowers it to 0.4253, still 2.00 times A/m.

3 Reporting volatility and identification

3.1 Period-level reporting variation

Replace H1 by a common period-specific reporting probability pt∈[0,1], independent of Rt and of n, with known mean ρ>0 and Var(pt)=ρ2τ2 (H5). Reporting remains independent across infections given pt. Because pt lies in [0,1] with mean ρ, Var(pt)≤ρ(1−ρ) [39], so τ2≤(1−ρ)/ρ. The estimator still divides by m=ρn and does not observe pt.

Proposition 2 (Reporting volatility and second-moment nonidentification). Under H2–H5, put Q=R¯2+vR. The first two moments of R̂t are:

E(R̂t)=R¯,Var(R̂t)=vR+vH+AHm,vH=τ2Q,AH=R¯+ρ(1+τ2)Qk.(10)

For known m, ρ and k, the single-period mean and variance in Eq. (10) depend on vR and τ2 only through U=(1+τ2)(R¯2+vR).

Given Rt and pt the estimator has mean (pt/ρ)Rt, so a shared reporting shock is not averaged away by more infections in the same period. The statement is deliberately narrow. It concerns the first two moments of one period’s count within the specified family. It does not exclude identification from full count distributions, from temporal structure under further assumptions, or from external measurements of reporting; it also assumes that reporting is independent of transmission, an assumption Section 6 relaxes.

Corollary 2 (Current and realised-mean risks with volatile reporting). Under H2–H5, the current-value risk is:

E[(R̂t−Rt)2]=vH+AHm.(11)

If, in addition, the pt are independent and identically distributed, independent of the transmission trajectory, and counts are independent given both trajectories, the two mean targets have risks:

E[(R̂¯T−R¯T)2]=vH+AH/mT,E[(R̂¯T−R¯)2]=BT+vH+AH/mT.(12)

At fixed T, unobserved reporting volatility leaves the floor vH/T on the realised-mean target as m grows, so a target free of transmission variation is not free of reporting error. The crossover scale with volatile reporting, m×,H=AH/(vR+vH), is never larger than m× (Eq. (A.5)); the lower crossover accompanies a larger risk, not better surveillance. Proofs are in Appendix A.4.

3.2 From the branching experiment to surveillance counts

If the scale m is random and associated with transmission, conditional unbiasedness given (Rt,m) still yields the conditional risk:

E[(R̂t−R¯)2∣m]=E(Rt∣m)+ρE(Rt2∣m)/km+Var(Rt∣m)+[E(Rt∣m)−R¯]2,(13)

and the conditional moments in Eq. (13) can change with scale. A constant intercept plus a constant coefficient on inverse count therefore does not follow when the count scale is itself an epidemic outcome, as it is in surveillance. Delays, aggregation, ratio denominators and changing conditional means further separate an apparent statistic from the experiment above. The rest of the paper accordingly treats empirical dispersion diagnostics as descriptive quantities and asks, with a written analysis plan and simulation checks, what they recover.

4 Data, diagnostic and analysis plan

4.1 Data and apparent reproduction number

We used the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) weekly hospital respiratory-data snapshot retrieved on 20 October 2026 and restricted influenza admissions to the 50 US states and the District of Columbia [40, 41]. Hospital participation varied during the series. Reporting was voluntary from May to October 2024 before it became mandatory again from 1 November 2024 [42], and the national Respiratory Illnesses Data Channel was not updated from 3 October to 13 November 2025 [43]. The analysis describes this surveillance system and does not estimate an effect of either event. Two external sources were added for the analyses of Section 4.6: state resident populations from the Census Bureau Vintage 2025 estimates [44], and the issue history of the same NHSN admission series from the Delphi Epidata archive [45], which records the first published and every revised value of each state-week count from November 2024 onwards.

The windows were the early-growth phases of four seasons: 1 October–26 November 2022, 7 October–23 December 2023, 9 November–28 December 2024 and 4 October–27 December 2025. Each is the contiguous national segment with weekly growth of at least 1.05 before the first turning point after the season’s admissible start; the 2024 start follows the return to mandatory reporting. The rule is applied identically to every season, and inference conditions on the selected windows. Sensitivity analyses use growth thresholds of 1.02 and 1.10 and fixed calendar windows for the first three seasons (8 October–26 November 2022, 14 October–16 December 2023 and 9 November 2024–18 January 2025). Missing or suppressed counts were kept missing rather than set to zero.

With Ct the admissions in week t, the apparent reproduction number of a state-week is the growth-to-reproduction transform:

RA,t=[max{0,1+(θ/7)log{(Ct+1+0.5)/(Ct+0.5)}}]α,α=(gμ/gσ)2,θ=gσ2/gμ.(14)

The transform follows the renewal relation between growth rate and reproduction number for a gamma-distributed interval [46]. It is not a true reproduction number or a posterior estimate from a renewal model [3, 10]. A row requires observed counts in weeks t and t+1 and Ct≥5, which leaves 1,748 state-weeks from 51 jurisdictions and 42 calendar weeks. The rows contain 1,969 distinct state-week counts in 210 runs of consecutive weeks.

The primary interval has mean gμ=3.6 days and standard deviation gσ=1.6 days, the household serial-interval estimate of Cowling et al. [47]. That estimate is a Weibull fit to 14 household transmission pairs; Eq. (14) uses the gamma distribution with the same mean and standard deviation. A serial interval is not a generation interval [48]. Sensitivity analyses set the mean to 3.2 and 4.0 days and the standard deviation to 1.2 and 2.0 days; the lower mean is close to the intrinsic generation-time estimate from US household data [49].

4.2 The diagnostic and its three summaries

For the apparent statistic X=RA with pooled mean X¯, the relative squared deviation and its affine working model are:

Lst=(Xst−X¯)2X¯2,E(Lst∣Cst)=a+bCst.(15)

This is the empirical counterpart of V(m)/R¯2 in Eq. (3), with a realised count in place of the expected scale and an apparent statistic in place of R̂t. It has the form of the additive overdispersion model of funnel plots [17, 18]. Three summaries of the fit follow.

The intercept a is the count-independent relative dispersion: all relative variation in X that does not scale with count. When reporting probabilities do not vary from week to week (τ=0), a estimates the relative variance of transmission, ṽR=vR/R¯2. When reporting shocks vary between weeks, a estimates ṽR+ṽH, where ṽH is the relative variance that the shocks induce in the ratio statistic (Appendix A.6). A reporting level that is constant over consecutive weeks cancels in the ratio, as it does in renewal estimators [2, 3]. By Proposition 2, single-period cross-sectional moments cannot separate the two components. The estimator also need not weight them equally: when the shocks are drawn independently for each state-week, the fitted intercept recovers only part of ṽH, and Section 5.6 quantifies the shortfall. The intercept is therefore read throughout as reflecting transmission and reporting variation, not as an estimate of their sum. It is also not an error floor for the current value: with τ=0 that floor is zero, and with τ>0 it is ṽH. For the process mean, a approximates the relative error that more cases cannot remove, to the extent that the affine form holds (Section 5.2).

The counting slope b is read against two references. A delta expansion of Eq. (14) under independent Poisson counts in consecutive weeks gives the independent-Poisson reference bP=κ(g)2[1+(Ct+0.5)/(Ct+1+0.5)]¯, a mean over rows, with κ(g)=(gμ/7)/[1+θlog(g)/7] and g=(Ct+1+0.5)/(Ct+0.5). Each row is evaluated at its own growth factor and normalised by X¯2, which approximates the expansion around X¯ when the row’s RA is close to X¯; bP is therefore a plug-in normalisation, not an exact expectation. For the primary sample bP=0.4455. Two alternatives show how much the normalisation matters. Replacing the unit normalisation by each row’s ratio Xst/X¯ gives 0.4199. The slope fitted to panels of independent Poisson counts drawn around the observed means, with the same transform, row filter and fit, gives 0.3977 (Table 12). The term 1 is the Poisson variance of the denominator count. In a branching chain the denominator week contains the parents of the numerator week, so conditioning on the realised parents leaves only the binomial reporting part of that variance, (1−ρ)/Ct. With Poisson offspring and reporting probability ρ this gives the branching-Poisson reference and its ratio to bP:

bP,br(ρ)=κ(g)2[(1−ρ)+(Ct+0.5)/(Ct+1+0.5)]¯,r(ρ)=bP,br(ρ)bP≈1+(1−ρ)g1+g=1−ρg1+g.(16)

Averaged over the observed rows, r(ρ) is 0.944, 0.861, 0.722 and 0.443 for ρ=0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 (Table S1). The observed-denominator model of Section 2.3 has the structure of the branching-Poisson reference, and the known-scale estimator of Section 2.1 is its limit without denominator noise. The ratio b/bP asks whether counting variation exceeds independent-Poisson noise; b/bP,br(ρ) asks the same for a branching chain, at a reporting probability that the data do not identify.

The third summary is the crossover count b/a, at which the fitted counting term equals the count-independent term. It is the empirical analogue of m× in admissions per week; m× refers to the expected count of a branching experiment. At C=b/a a shrinkage estimator of the Fay–Herriot type places half its weight on the direct estimate (Eq. (5)). Table 4 lists the conditions under which each summary identifies its theoretical counterpart and the direction of distortion when they fail.

When reporting varies (τ>0), a reflects both ṽR and ṽH; in simulation its estimate fell 6–22% short of their sum (Section 5.6). It does not identify ṽR and is not an error floor. 4.3 Estimation and inference

The affine mean was fitted by iterated feasible generalised least squares with weights inversely proportional to the squared fitted mean, which minimises a gamma quasi-deviance; this is an estimating criterion, not a distributional claim. The primary interval is the two-way cluster-robust sandwich of Cameron et al. [50] for the stacked estimating equations of X¯ and the affine fit, clustered by state and calendar week, with small-sample factors G/(G−1) and critical values from the t distribution on 41 degrees of freedom, one fewer than the number of weeks. The interval for b/a is formed on the log scale. Two resampling checks accompany it: a calendar-week block bootstrap (1,999 draws) that resamples whole weeks with all their state rows, and a wild cluster bootstrap-t over calendar weeks with six-point weights and the null a=0 imposed (9,999 draws) [51, 52]. In the wild bootstrap, losses at or below 10−7 in a bootstrap sample are set to 10−7 before the restricted fit; this affected 13.5% of bootstrap rows, and Table S12 reports the test under other thresholds and without the clamp. The state-by-week pigeonhole bootstrap [53] used for the supplementary analyses is conservative on this design: under the fresh-draw generators of Section 4.5 its standard deviation of â was 1.55–1.78 times the Monte Carlo standard deviation (Table S13). Every interval quoted in the text is listed with its type and source in Table S14; all are 95% intervals, and an interval without a stated type has the type of the nearest preceding interval of the same paragraph.

4.4 Analysis plan and primary test

The analysis plan was written after an exploratory analysis of the same data, and it lists the estimates and the season-test p values that were then known, so that each choice can be judged against them. It was fixed, with a checksum, before any analysis in Section 5 was run. Because the data had been seen, the plan does not make the primary test confirmatory in the sense of an untouched hypothesis; what it fixes is the robustness rule for the intercept, the primary calibration of the season test and the obligation to report every specified analysis. The data vintage, the sample and RA with the primary interval were frozen.

The primary test (E1) is of H0:a=0 against a two-sided alternative at α=0.05, tested with the two-way sandwich t statistic on 41 degrees of freedom. The claim that count-independent dispersion remains is called robust only if the primary test rejects and the 95% lower limit of a stays above zero in each of nine sensitivity analyses. Two vary the generation-interval mean (S-a1) and standard deviation (S-a2). Three change the row filters: count floors of 10, 20 and 50 (S-a3), the fixed calendar windows (S-a4) and growth thresholds (S-a5). Three remove data: transitions that touch the 2025 data-channel interruption (S-a6), one season at a time (S-a7) and rows with hospital reporting coverage below 90% in either week (S-a8). The last (S-a9) removes one calendar week at a time to measure influence.

A within-week intercept (E3) is a different estimand, not a sensitivity analysis. It replaces X¯ by the mean of the same calendar week computed without the row’s own state, which removes common national variation by week; the week mean including the own row and a version that also rescales by the week mean are reported as alternatives. Its interval is the calendar-week block bootstrap.

The secondary test asks whether season intercepts differ. In a model with four season intercepts as and a common slope, H0:loga1=…=loga4 is tested with the Wald statistic WCGM that uses the two-way sandwich covariance. The season label is constant within a calendar week, so it is assigned at the level of 42 weeks in four groups. With few clusters at the level of assignment, wild cluster bootstrap tests can be badly mis-sized and randomisation inference at that level is recommended [54, 55]. The primary reference distribution is therefore a permutation of season labels across calendar weeks that keeps the number of weeks per season (9,999 permutations); it assumes exchangeable weeks and ignores serial dependence between adjacent weeks. The season difference is called significant only if this p<0.05, whatever the other calibrations show. All other calibrations are reported, and Holm-adjusted p values over E1 and the season test are given. Season intercepts are interpreted only as reflecting transmission and reporting variation together (Proposition 2).

The counting slope b/bP, the crossover count and the predicted relative squared error a+b/C at C=10, 37, 100 and 1,000 were specified for estimation, without tests.

4.5 Simulation checks

The conversion of a into a transmission standard deviation needs a mechanism. For a simulated mechanism with recovery ratio r=E(â)/ṽR, the implied relative standard deviation of the reproduction number is (a/r)1/2. Its interval combines the two-way interval of a with the Monte Carlo 2.5–97.5% range of r. The plan required that this quantity be reported as a grid over mechanisms and never as a single estimate, and that a1/2 be described as a relative standard deviation of transmission and reporting variation combined, not of transmission alone. A mechanism reproduces the counting slope when its Monte Carlo 2.5–97.5% range of b/bP contains the observed value. Synthetic panels are generated on the exact design of the data. The expected count level is calibrated to the observed median retained count of 45, and the heterogeneity amplitude is calibrated so that the mean fitted intercept equals the observed a (Appendix C). Five checks with fixed criteria were specified:

  • SC1, two generations per week: a daily renewal process with the primary generation interval, Poisson or negative binomial (k=0.3) offspring and weekly binomial reporting at ρ∈{0.003,0.01,0.1}. The one-generation recovery map carries over if E(â)/vR lies in [0.8,1.25] in every cell.

  • SC2 and SC3, reporting and offspring dispersion: a grid of ρ∈{0.001,0.003,0.01,0.03,0.1,0.25,0.5,1} and k∈{0.1,0.3,1,3,∞} with independent transmission heterogeneity, 100 panels per cell. SC2 requires intercept recovery in [0.9,1.1] in every cell; SC3 requires the mean of b/bP to lie in [0.9,1.1] in every cell with ρ≤0.01. The range ρ=0.001–0.01 for the probability that an infection becomes a reported admission is assumed from burden estimates [56, 57], not estimated.

  • SC4 and SC5, interval validity: these use generators that redraw the heterogeneity field in every replicate. FD-S1 has independent heterogeneity, and FD-S8 has scale-dependent heterogeneity with state-week reporting shocks. FD-S9 adds to FD-S8 a national calendar-week share of 0.25, 0.5 or 0.75 of the heterogeneity; this family was defined after the data had been seen. SC4 requires coverage of E(â) by the two-way interval of at least 0.90 under every generator. SC5 calls the gap between the observed standard error of a and the generators’ Monte Carlo standard deviation explained if their ratio lies in [0.67,1.5] for at least one generator.

4.6 Amendments and additional analyses

The plan was amended twice, and both amendments are distributed with it. Amendment 1 recorded implementation details that the plan had left open: seeds, the restricted fit and loss clamp of the wild bootstrap, and the construction of the daily-renewal generator. It stated that these details were fixed before the full runs, but the run logs show that the full runs of the primary test, the season test and the simulation checks had finished before it was written. The details were already in the code used for those runs, and no evidence was found that any of them was changed after a result was seen. The season script was edited once after its first full run. The text of that edit could not be recovered, but every quantity logged by both runs is identical, including the primary permutation p value, the other calibrations, the data sensitivities and the power analysis.

Amendment 2 was fixed, with a checksum, before any of the following analyses was run. Each is secondary or descriptive, none can change the verdict of the primary test, the significance level, the calibration or the data, and each was specified with its reading rule.

  • Functional form. The observed mean loss in each decile of Ct, with a calendar-week block-bootstrap interval, is compared with the affine fit, a power law cC−γ and a three-parameter model a+bC−γ. The intercept is said to survive a free exponent if the block-bootstrap interval of a in the three-parameter model excludes zero; γ=1 is called compatible with the data if its interval contains one.

  • Model-free floor. Among rows with Ct at or above the 75th, 90th and 95th percentiles, the mean loss minus the mean counting term, with either b̂ or bP as the slope, estimates the count-independent component without extrapolation.

  • Population size. The intercept is made linear in the standardised log population z of the jurisdiction, a0+a1z, with a common slope, and a1=0 is tested with the two-way sandwich on 41 degrees of freedom. If the interval of a1 lies below zero, statements about what more cases buy are restricted to jurisdictions of comparable size and the error at a given count is reported by population tertile. A log-link intercept, a slope that also varies with z, and separate fits by tertile are secondary.

  • Bias of the intercept. Under the fresh-draw generators with reporting shocks, and in a sweep of the transmission share of their variance (1, 0.75, 0.25), the relative bias E(â)/(ṽR+ṽH)−1 and the weight wH that solves E(â)=ṽR+wHṽH are estimated. If every bias interval excludes zero, â is described as reflecting, not estimating, the total.

  • Generator realism. Six cells of a state-realistic generator anchor transmission to the smoothed observed epidemic curve, scale its variance by state and allow clustered admissions. Four tests compare the Monte Carlo range of each cell with the data: the slope ratio b/bP (T1), the 90th percentile of Ct (T2), the ratio of pooled to within-state slope (T3) and the between-state coefficient of variation of the intercepts (T4). The generators reproduce the data if all four pass in one cell. Their design used the observed slope and between-state dispersion, and no inferential result rests on them.

  • Reporting data. The fit is repeated with counts scaled by the share of hospitals reporting in each state-week, and on the first-issue and latest-issue counts of the archive for the 661 rows whose first issue is provisional.

  • Calibration details. The wild bootstrap is repeated under four loss clamps and without one; the standard deviation of the pigeonhole bootstrap is compared with the Monte Carlo standard deviation of â (it is called conservative only if the ratio exceeds one under every fresh-draw generator); and b/bP is reported under the three Poisson references.

5 Results for US influenza hospital admissions

5.1 A count-independent floor

The pooled affine fit of Eq. (15) gave a=0.0150 (two-way 95% CI 0.0109–0.0191; t41=7.36, two-sided p=5.1×10−9) and b=0.560 (0.430–0.690) (Table 5). The primary test (E1) rejects a=0, and the Holm-adjusted p over the two tests of the plan is 1.0×10−8. The secondary calibrations agree. Clustering by state alone or by week alone gave intervals of 0.0125–0.0174 and 0.0112–0.0188. The week-cluster wild bootstrap-t with the null imposed gave p=0.0001, the smallest value attainable with 9,999 draws, at every clamp of the bootstrap losses from 10−9 to 10−3 and 0.0003 without a clamp (Table S12). None of the 1,999 calendar-week block-bootstrap draws gave a≤0 (block-bootstrap percentile interval 0.0107–0.0192).

The lower limit of a stayed above zero in every sensitivity analysis of the plan, so the claim meets the robustness rule (Fig. 2). Point estimates ranged from 0.0117 to 0.0202 over 17 specifications, and the smallest lower limit, 0.0082, came from leaving out the 2025–26 season. The generation interval moved a most: a mean of 3.2 days gave 0.0117 and a mean of 4.0 days gave 0.0186, because the transform (14) rescales all deviations together. Raising the count floor lowered a slightly, to 0.0130 (0.0088–0.0172) at Ct≥50 on 828 rows. The fixed calendar windows gave the widest interval, 0.0092–0.0311, on 1,263 rows from three seasons. Leaving out one calendar week at a time gave estimates of 0.0136–0.0156 with a smallest lower limit of 0.0100. Count-independent dispersion is therefore present in these data under every specification that the plan fixed, provided the decline with count is inverse; Section 5.2 examines that proviso.

5.2 How well the affine form fits

The affine form describes the decline of the loss with count only approximately (Table S10; Fig. 3). Across deciles of the current-week count the mean loss fell from 0.0684 to 0.0110, and the affine prediction lay outside the block-bootstrap interval of the observed mean in three of ten deciles: above it in the lowest decile (0.0906 against 0.0538–0.0854) and in the highest (0.0158 against 0.0079–0.0137), and below it in the fifth (0.0296 against 0.0310–0.0501). A fit a+bC−γ with a free exponent lowered the quasi-deviance by 10.67, and the gain exceeded 2 in 94.6% of calendar-week block-bootstrap draws (Table 6). Its exponent was γ=0.617 (week bootstrap 0.355–0.870; state bootstrap 0.438–0.862), so the inverse-count decline γ=1 lies outside both intervals. Its intercept was 0.0089, and the week-bootstrap interval reached zero (−0.0014 to 0.0137; 4.0% of draws at or below zero), whereas the state-bootstrap interval did not (0.0034–0.0144). Under the reading rule fixed in Amendment 2 the floor therefore does not survive a free exponent. Within the observed counts a slower decline with a smaller constant and an inverse decline with a larger constant describe the data almost equally well, and the intercept of either model is an extrapolation beyond the largest counts.

The rows with the largest counts give the floor without a model for the decline (Table 6; Fig. 4). Among the 175 state-weeks at or above the 90th percentile of the count (Ct≥389, mean 882) the mean loss was 0.0110 (week bootstrap 0.0078–0.0139), a relative root mean squared deviation of 10.5% (8.8–11.8%). Subtracting the counting term with the fitted slope left 0.0102 (0.0069–0.0132), a relative standard deviation of 10.1% (8.3–11.5%), and subtracting it with the Poisson reference left 0.0104 (0.0071–0.0132). At the 75th and 95th percentiles the net relative standard deviation was 11.8% (9.8–13.2%) and 9.8% (8.0–11.1%). At the largest observed counts, therefore, a count-independent relative error of about 10% remains, and all of these intervals exclude zero. The model-free value at the 90th percentile lies between the three-parameter intercept and the affine one.

5.3 What more cases buy

The observed relative error fell with count but levelled off at large counts (Table S10). The relative root mean squared deviation of RA was 26.2% in the lowest count decile (mean 7.8 admissions a week), 20.1% in the fifth (mean 38.5), 14.9% in the seventh (mean 93.5) and 10.5% in the highest (mean 882). A ninefold increase in the mean count from the seventh to the tenth decile thus lowered the relative error by about four percentage points. The affine model gives smooth values over the same range, 26.6% at 10 admissions, 17.3% at 37 and 14.3% at 100 (Table 7). Its extrapolation to 1,000 admissions, 12.5%, exceeds the observed relative error of the highest decile, so statements about large counts here rest on the model-free floor of Section 5.2. The crossover count, at which the two affine terms are equal, was b/a=37.4 admissions a week (two-way 24.1–58.3; block bootstrap 23.4–60.5). It rose to 46.1, 48.6 and 51.5 at count floors of 10, 20 and 50 and lay between 25.6 and 55.5 across the other sensitivity analyses, so its order of magnitude, a few tens of weekly admissions, is stable while its value is not. It is an in-sample balance point for this panel, not a sample-size rule for surveillance.

These values pool jurisdictions whose count-independent component differs (Section 5.4). Separate affine fits by population tertile gave predicted relative errors at 37, 100 and 390 admissions of 18.3, 15.6 and 14.2% in the smallest-population tertile, 17.9, 15.5 and 14.4% in the middle tertile and 16.2, 13.5 and 12.1% in the largest. What additional cases buy should be judged against the component of the jurisdiction concerned.

5.4 Jurisdiction size

The intercept fell with state population (Table 8; Fig. 5). In the Amendment 2 model with an intercept linear in standardised log population and a common slope, the population coefficient was a1=−0.0054 per standard deviation (two-way −0.0085 to −0.0023; t41=−3.51, p=0.0011), and its state-bootstrap and week-bootstrap intervals also excluded zero. The fitted intercept was 0.0273 at the 10th percentile of population (0.92 million) and 0.0137 at the 90th (12.7 million), a ratio of 0.50 (state bootstrap 0.41–0.61); a log-link intercept gave a ratio of 0.44 (state bootstrap 0.32–0.60). The counting slope did not change detectably with population (coefficient −0.015; two-way −0.124 to 0.095). Separate fits by tertile gave intercepts of 0.0189 (two-way 0.0145–0.0233), 0.0195 (0.0125–0.0264) and 0.0135 (0.0090–0.0180), and with a common slope the ratio of the largest-population to the smallest-population tertile was 0.60 (state bootstrap 0.42–0.82).

Population and count go together in this panel: the median count was 20, 37 and 106 admissions in the three tertiles. Because the affine form overpredicts the loss at the largest counts (Section 5.2), part of the population gradient may reflect that misfit rather than a property of the jurisdictions. Either way the pooled intercept of 0.0150 is an average over jurisdictions whose count-independent component differs about twofold, and the count beyond which more cases help little is specific to the jurisdiction.

5.5 What the floor contains

Removing common national variation by calendar week lowered the intercept to 0.0102 (block bootstrap 0.0078–0.0126) with the leave-state-out week centre, a reduction of 32.0% (10.2–47.8) (Table 7). With the week centre including the own row the reduction was 34.7% (13.8–49.8), and with week-specific centre and scale it was 42.6% (22.0–57.0). Centring by season removed 1.6% (−6.8 to 19.1). About a third of the floor is thus shared by states in the same week, and about two thirds varies between states within a week. The within-week intercept stays above zero under every centring.

The floor reflects transmission and reporting variation, and its transmission share is not identified. The square root of a, 12.2%, is the relative standard deviation of the non-counting variation that the intercept captures around the pooled mean, which can fall short of the sum of the two sources (Section 5.6). Converting a into a transmission standard deviation requires a mechanism, and across 71 simulated mechanisms the implied relative standard deviation of the reproduction number ranged from 8.6% to 18.6%, with propagated intervals from 6.9% to 22.7% (Table 9; Fig. 6). Restricted to the 13 mechanisms that reproduce the observed counting slope, the range was 8.6–13.9%. Reporting shocks make the intercept overstate transmission variance, and heterogeneity that shrinks with count makes it understate it, which is why the range is wide in both directions.

The mapping itself depends on the time scale of transmission (SC1). Under a daily renewal process with the primary generation interval, about two generations fall within a week, and the intercept recovered 75–78% of the variance of the weekly reproduction number, outside the range of 0.8–1.25 fixed in the plan. Against the mean of two consecutive weekly values it recovered 150–156%. The one-generation map of Section 2 therefore does not carry over unchanged to weekly hospital counts, and the implied standard deviations above inherit this dependence.

5.6 How the intercept relates to its sources

Under fresh-draw generators the intercept tracked transmission variance when there was no reporting shock and fell short of the total when there was (Table 10). With independent heterogeneity (FD-S1) its relative bias against vR+vH was +1.4% (panel bootstrap 0.5–2.3%). Under FD-S8, in which about half of the calibrated variance is a reporting shock, it was −14.2% (−15.1 to −13.3%), and under the three post hoc variants FD-S9 it was −13.8 to −14.9%. Varying the transmission share of the FD-S8 variance moved the shortfall from 22.1% at a share of 0.75 to 6.3% at a share of 0.25, and with no reporting shock in that family the intercept recovered 0.707 of the transmission variance. The weight of the reporting variance in E(â)=vR+wHvH ranged from 0.10 to 0.91 across these laws. The direction of the bias is downward under every law with reporting shocks, and its size depends on the share and mechanism, neither of which the data identify. The intercept is therefore not rescaled, which would give 0.0160–0.0192 depending on the law, and it is read as reflecting transmission and reporting variation rather than as an estimate of their sum.

Mechanism-conditional rescaling aobs/tg would range 0.0160–0.0192; not used.

5.7 External reporting data

Two external sources bound parts of the reporting component (Table 11). Hospital participation averaged 92.9% of hospitals per jurisdiction-week (minimum 67.7%) and changed by 0.78 percentage points between consecutive weeks on average. Scaling both counts by participation lowered a by 0.00029, or 2.0% (week bootstrap −0.00086 to 0.00027), so changing participation explains little of the intercept. Revisions explain more. In the Delphi Epidata archive of issues [45], which starts with week 47 of 2024, 661 rows had a provisional first issue in both weeks. The first issue equalled the latest in 29.2% of them, was revised upward in 65.8% and downward in 5.0%, and the mean relative revision was 11.0%. On the 654 rows with both counts at least 5, a was 0.0227 (block bootstrap 0.0133–0.0298) with first-issue counts and 0.0143 (0.0096–0.0183) with latest-issue counts, a difference of 0.0084 (0.0016–0.0146). Counts available in real time thus carry a count-independent component about 1.6 times that of settled counts. Neither source measures the reporting error that remains in settled counts, so the transmission share of a stays unidentified.

5.8 Counting slope, reporting and offspring dispersion

The counting slope was 1.257 times the plug-in independent-Poisson reference bP (block bootstrap 0.97–1.59). That reference normalises every row by the squared pooled mean; normalising each row by its own ratio to the pooled mean lowers bP from 0.4455 to 0.4199 and raises the ratio by 6.1% to 1.334 (two-way, reference fixed, 1.02–1.64). An exact reference simulated from Poisson counts on the same design gives 0.3977 and a ratio of 1.408 (1.08–1.73) (Table 12). Whether counting variation exceeds independent Poisson noise therefore depends on the reference: under the plug-in reference used in the plan it is not shown, and under the other two the lower limit lies just above 1. The comparisons with simulated slopes below use the plug-in reference throughout, so they are not affected. Against the branching-Poisson reference of Eq. (16) the point ratio would be 1.46 at ρ=0.25 and 2.84 at ρ=1 (Table S1), but the slope does not identify ρ. Within-state fits were less precise: a state fixed-effects fit gave 0.85 (0.24–1.47) times bP and a week fixed-effects fit 1.42 (0.96–1.89) (Table S6).

The reporting-by-offspring grid shows what the slope can and cannot reveal (Table 13; Fig. 7). Intercept recovery stayed within 0.9–1.1 at ρ≤0.25 for every offspring law and at all ρ for k≥1, but rose to 1.18 at ρ=0.5 and 1.49 at ρ=1 with k=0.1, and to 1.11 at ρ=1 with k=0.3; SC2 therefore fails, in cells outside the assumed range of ρ. In the assumed range, ρ≤0.01, the expected slope ratio was 0.85–0.91 whatever the offspring law, below 1 rather than within 0.9–1.1 as SC3 required. Offspring dispersion cannot be read from the counting slope at realistic reporting probabilities, and no cell in that range reproduces the observed 1.257. Only three of 40 cells did, all with ρ≥0.1 and k≤0.3. The observed slope is thus compatible with strong overdispersion only at reporting probabilities far above those of hospital surveillance, or with counting variation that the simulated mechanisms do not contain.

5.9 Season intercepts

No difference between season intercepts was detected under the primary calibration (calendar-week permutation p=0.102; power 0.47 at the observed pattern). The Wald statistic was WCGM=17.8 on 3 degrees of freedom, and its calendar-week permutation p was 0.102 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.003) (Table 14; Fig. 8B). Season statements below are therefore exploratory. The other calibrations disagree with one another. The asymptotic χ32 reference gave p=0.0005, the week-cluster wild bootstrap 0.011, the state-cluster wild bootstrap 0.013, the within-state permutation 0.045, generator-based references 0.005–0.055, the bootstrap-covariance statistic 0.138 and circular shifts of the season sequence 0.405. The state-level calibrations treat states as independent clusters although the season label varies only between weeks, and the generator-based ones depend on the simulated mechanism. Under the primary calibration, excluding the 2025 data-channel interruption gave p=0.261, restricting to rows with at least 90% reporting coverage gave 0.081, and the fixed calendar windows for three seasons gave 0.031.

The 2023–24 intercept was the lowest, 0.0071 (two-way sandwich on the log scale, 0.0050–0.0100), against 0.0154–0.0180 in the other seasons (Table 15; Fig. 8A). The ratio of the highest to the lowest intercept was 2.54 (season-stratified block bootstrap 1.75–4.35), an estimate that is biased upward. A contrast of 2023–24 against the other seasons, chosen after the data had been seen, gave a ratio of 0.43 (two-way sandwich on the log scale, 0.29–0.65) and is not tested. Power at the observed pattern was 0.47 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.025), and 80% power would need a highest-to-lowest ratio of about 4.5 (Fig. 8C). With equal season intercepts the test rejected in 0.0625 of simulated panels (Monte Carlo standard error 0.012), about one standard error above the nominal 0.05. This power curve uses a loss-level statistic whose permutation critical value, 17.65, is lower than that of the primary test, so it is probably optimistic. The absence of a detected difference is therefore weak evidence that the season intercepts are equal. With four seasons the design can detect only large differences, and the between-season variance itself cannot be estimated precisely (Appendix B.3).

Any season difference would be a difference in the combined transmission and reporting variation that the intercept reflects. Mean hospital reporting coverage of the sample rows was 90.9–94.2% in every season (Table 15), but coverage does not measure the reporting probability per infection, and scaling counts by participation changed a by 2.0% (Section 5.7). Reporting regimes did differ outside the analysis windows: median participation in summer 2024, when reporting was voluntary, was 45.6% against 92.3–94.2% in the other summers (Table S7).

5.10 Validity of the intervals

Under generators that redraw the heterogeneity field in every replicate, the two-way interval covered the mean of â in 0.920–0.975 of panels, which meets SC4 (Table 16). Its mean standard error was 0.92–1.07 times the Monte Carlo standard deviation. Under mechanisms with reporting shocks the interval is centred on an estimator that falls short of the total (Section 5.6), and it covered the true total in only 0.44–0.59 of panels, against 0.975 under independent heterogeneity. The observed standard error of a was 1.53–2.08 times the Monte Carlo standard deviation under the fresh-draw laws of the plan and 1.39 under the national-share law with share 0.75, which was defined after the data had been seen. SC5 is therefore met only by a post hoc law. The two-way interval is wider than the Monte Carlo spread under every fresh-draw law, and the pigeonhole bootstrap standard deviation was 1.55–1.78 times it (Table S13), so the intervals reported here are conservative for the mean of â under these laws.

Generators built to reproduce the state structure of the panel did not close the gap between the variability of the data and of the simulated panels (Table S11). They combined a transmission field around a smoothed observed trend, with state-specific variance proportional to the population-dependent intercept or to state intercepts, clustered admissions and a reporting probability of 0.01 or 0.003. In five of the six cells the smoothed trend alone exceeded the transmission target, so the transmission standard deviation could not be calibrated. No cell reproduced all four tested features of the observed panel: the counting slope ratio fell inside the Monte Carlo range only without admission clustering, the 90th percentile of the count in five of six cells, the pooled-to-within-state slope ratio (T3) in none and the between-state spread of intercepts in all. Under these cells the two-way interval covered the mean of â in 0.96–1.00 of panels, the observed standard error was 1.63–2.31 times the Monte Carlo standard deviation, and the intercept captured 70–78% of the simulated non-counting total, which the interval covered in only 0.015–0.16 of panels. Which features of the data inflate its variability relative to these mechanisms remains unexplained. Simulated null distributions for the season test, which drew on generators with a fixed heterogeneity field, gave p values of 0.005–0.045; redrawing the field raised them to 0.035–0.055. These generator-based calibrations are not used as evidence for season differences.

6 Discussion

The theoretical part of the paper makes one distinction precise. With fixed, known reporting, exogenous exposure and conditionally independent counting errors, the risk for the current value is A/m and the risk for the realised mean of the observed periods is A/(Tm). The process mean adds the variance of the realised mean, which more cases within the same periods do not reduce. The count at which counting error equals between-period variance is the half-weight point of the corresponding shrinkage estimator, as in small-area estimation and disease mapping [14, 15]. It belongs with its estimator, target and sampling experiment and is not a property of a pathogen. The efficiency statement holds within a class of conditionally unbiased estimators with a known denominator. Information from other features of the epidemic curve [6, 58], independent reporting measurements or prior structure changes what can be learned, and estimators that accept bias in exchange for lower variance lie outside that class. Appendix B gives the corresponding forecast weight, the allocation of a fixed budget between periods and cases, and a lower bound on the precision with which a few seasons can estimate between-season variation.

The application answers its primary question. US influenza hospital admissions in early-growth weeks carry a count-independent component of squared relative error: the primary test rejected a=0, the lower limit stayed above zero in every sensitivity analysis of the plan, and about two thirds of the component remains after common calendar-week variation is removed. Its size is better read from the data than from the affine model, which fits the decline with count only approximately. Among the state-weeks with the largest counts the relative error of a weekly apparent reproduction number was about 10%, almost none of it counting noise, whereas in the lowest count decile it was 26%. Beyond a few tens of weekly admissions, more cases mainly buy precision for the current value of a statistic whose remaining spread is not counting noise. This is the empirical counterpart of the distinction between targets: a count-based precision statement describes the first component and is silent on the second. The component is not common to all jurisdictions. It was about half as large in the most populous states as in the least populous, so a single pooled intercept understates the error in small jurisdictions and overstates it in large ones.

What the count-independent component is cannot be settled from these data. Its transmission share is not identified (Proposition 2), and implied transmission standard deviations ranged from 8.6% to 18.6% across simulated mechanisms, a grid that depends on the assumed mechanism and on the number of generations per week. Under reporting shocks the intercept fell 6–22% short of the transmission-plus-reporting total, so it combines the two sources with unequal weights rather than adding them. The counting slope, its ratio to the independent-Poisson or branching-Poisson reference and the thinning response also cannot distinguish overdispersed offspring, under-reporting and heterogeneous transmission. At reporting probabilities typical of hospital admissions the expected slope ratio was below one whatever the offspring law. The observed ratio was 1.26 against the plug-in reference used throughout and 1.33–1.41 against two closer approximations, so whether counting variation exceeds independent Poisson noise depends on the reference. No difference between season intercepts was detected under the primary calibration (p=0.102; power 0.47). The lower intercept of 2023–24 is a hypothesis for data with more seasons or with external reporting measurements, not a finding, and the power analysis shows that four seasons can detect only differences of about fourfold or more. The crossover count of about 37 admissions per week marks where counting noise stops dominating the cross-sectional dispersion of this statistic in the pooled panel, not where additional cases stop being useful for a particular target.

6.1 Real-time estimation

All main analyses used a retrospective snapshot in which counts are close to final. In real time, reporting delays leave the most recent weeks incomplete, and right-censoring biases the latest counts downwards in proportion to the delay distribution [59, 60]. In the archived issues of these data two thirds of first-issue counts were later revised upward, and the intercept computed from first-issue counts was about 1.6 times that from settled counts (Section 5.7). The current-value target is affected first and most, because its risk is dominated by the last one or two periods, exactly those that are incomplete, whereas a realised or process mean over many periods dilutes them. The RA statistic also needs Ct+1, so it is available only one week after its reference week, and estimates near the end of a series combine smaller effective counts with nowcasting uncertainty. Real-time renewal methods address this by modelling delays and the infection process jointly [2, 61, 62]. In the present framework, nowcasting adds a correction-error term to the counting term, and its variance grows as the delay distribution places more mass beyond the current week. Error statements derived from settled data will therefore overstate the precision available in real time.

Estimation windows raise a related issue. Widening a window in renewal estimators accumulates incidence while imposing constancy of the reproduction number over a longer interval [2, 3]. This trades temporal resolution for precision and is not equivalent to observing more independent periods; the averages in Table 2 instead give each period its own transmission value. Applying their formulas to overlapping windows requires explicit treatment of the overlap.

6.2 Reporting that depends on transmission

Proposition 2 assumes that the reporting probability is independent of transmission. In practice testing, care seeking and admission thresholds can change with epidemic activity [63, 64]. Write zt=pt/ρ for the relative reporting probability. Given Rt, the estimator then has conditional bias

E(R̂t∣Rt)−Rt=[E(zt∣Rt)−1]Rt.(17)

By Eq. (17), if reporting rises with transmission, so that Cov(zt,Rt)>0, high-transmission periods are over-counted and low-transmission periods under-counted, the estimated swings exaggerate the true ones, and the fitted intercept overstates the relative dispersion of transmission. If reporting falls with transmission, for example when admission capacity saturates or testing is rationed at the peak, the estimates damp the swings and the intercept understates it. In both cases the process-mean estimate is biased by Cov(zt,Rt), and the bias does not shrink with more cases. Neither direction can be detected from the counts alone; it requires external information on testing or admission practice. The participation adjustment used here addresses only facility participation, and it changed the intercept by 2.0% (Section 5.7).

6.3 Choice of interval distribution

The transform in Eq. (14) needs an interval distribution. The household serial interval of Cowling et al. [47] was kept as the primary choice because it is directly estimated for influenza and widely used; it rests on 14 transmission pairs. The intrinsic generation-time estimate of Chan et al. [49], the more appropriate quantity for a renewal mapping, is close to the lower mean of the sensitivity analysis. Serial intervals, intrinsic generation intervals and realised household generation intervals are different quantities [48], and the mapping from growth rate to reproduction number depends on which is used [46]. The interval rescales all deviations: a mean of 3.2 days gave a=0.0117 and a mean of 4.0 days gave 0.0186, whereas the crossover count stayed between 37.4 and 37.6 and the slope ratio between 1.23 and 1.28 (Table 5). The level of a therefore depends on this choice, and the conclusion that it exceeds zero and the balance between the two error terms do not.

6.4 Identification and limitations

Separating the mechanisms behind the dispersion curve requires information that a single cross-section lacks. Temporal structure can separate persistent transmission variation from independent counting and reporting noise under explicit state-space or renewal models [34, 35, 65], and external measurements of reporting can constrain ρ and its variation. The shape of the curve narrows the candidates without identifying one. In the known-truth audit (Appendix C), no generator reproduced all features of the data. The generators that came closest combined scale-dependent heterogeneity with reporting shocks, and generators built on the state structure of the panel also failed to reproduce it, which leaves the transmission share of a open. The affine form is an approximation. It missed the observed mean loss in three of ten count deciles, and a free count exponent fitted better and moved the intercept towards zero. The held-out comparison did not favour the affine form over a power law (contrast −0.0020, standard error 0.0068; Table S8). The affine intercept is therefore a summary within the observed counts, and the model-free floor at the largest counts is the more direct measure of the count-independent component. Reporting that varies with jurisdiction size would leave the same trace as scale-dependent transmission, and the population gradient of the intercept cannot be attributed to either.

The growth windows are a fixed rule applied to four seasons of one surveillance system, and inference conditions on that selection. Transfer to other epidemic regimes would need data from those regimes. The analysis plan followed exploratory analysis of the same data (Section 4.4), and the primary test of a=0 was already clear at that stage. The plan therefore does not make that test confirmatory. Its value lies in the robustness rule, the season-test calibration and the complete reporting of every planned analysis. The analyses of the second amendment were planned after the first set of results and are secondary. The main analyses used a retrospective snapshot, so reporting delays and right-censoring of recent weeks were not modelled (Section 6.1). Not all simulation checks passed. With about two generations per week the intercept recovered three quarters of the variance of the weekly reproduction number. With near-complete reporting and strong offspring dispersion it overstated that variance, and in the assumed reporting range the counting slope carried no information on offspring dispersion. The two-way interval for a covered its expectation under every redrawn generator. Under reporting shocks, however, it covered the true transmission-plus-reporting total in only about half of the panels, and the observed standard error exceeded the simulated variability under all laws of the plan and under the state-structured generators. As statements about the total, intervals for a therefore under-cover, although the lower limit lies far above zero. Intervals for iterated fits condition on convergence, and within-state slopes were imprecise. Facility participation and revisions measure only parts of ascertainment, and the reporting error that remains in settled counts is not identified from public data.

6.5 Checklist for surveillance practice

Four recommendations for reporting reproduction numbers follow from these results.

  1. State the inferential target. An estimate may target the current value Rt, the realised mean R¯T over the observed periods or the process mean R¯. Precision statements of the form A/m apply to the first two under declared reporting assumptions and omit between-period variation for the third.

  2. Inflate the counting error when the denominator is an observed count. The delta factor is 1+(1−ρ)(R¯2+vR)/A, which is 1.48 under the illustrative parameters of Section 2.3. At small counts the factor is larger, 2.42 at m=10 in Table 3. The half-weight count of the shrinkage estimator moves from m× to m×+(1−ρ)(R¯2+vR)/vR, from 53.1 to 78.6 under the same parameters.

  3. Qualify single-period estimates for reporting volatility. One period’s counts cannot separate transmission changes from reporting shocks (Proposition 2), so rapid changes should be checked against testing volumes, reporting participation or temporal models before they are interpreted as transmission.

  4. Treat dispersion fits as descriptive, report their intercept and estimate it by jurisdiction. The intercept a, the slope b and the crossover count b/a describe the observed statistic on the selected rows. A positive intercept shows that counting error is not the whole error, but it reflects transmission and reporting variation, not a transmission-variance estimate without an assumed mechanism. It differed about twofold between small and large jurisdictions here, so the count-independent component added to the counting error should be specific to the jurisdiction, and b/a is not a sample-size threshold for surveillance.

7 Conclusion

The inferential target decides what additional cases buy. More cases shrink the counting error of the current value and of the realised mean of the observed periods, but they do not remove the between-period variation that limits estimation of the process mean, and with an observed denominator the counting error is larger than the known-scale formula implies. In US influenza hospital admissions the primary test found a count-independent component of squared relative error that stayed above zero under every sensitivity analysis of the plan. Its size is better read from the data than from the affine extrapolation: among the state-weeks with the largest counts the relative error of an apparent reproduction number was about 10%, and counting noise contributed little of it. The component was about twice as large in small as in large jurisdictions, so the count beyond which more cases help little is a property of the jurisdiction rather than a common constant. It reflects transmission and reporting variation without separating them, can understate their sum, and was larger for first-issue counts than for settled ones. Precision statements for reproduction numbers should therefore name their target and add a jurisdiction-specific count-independent component to the counting error; separating its sources requires temporal models or external data on reporting.

Data and code availability

The analyses used the dataset Weekly Hospital Respiratory Data (HRD) Metrics by Jurisdiction, National Healthcare Safety Network, published by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention under the identifier ua7e-t2fy [40], in the snapshot retrieved on 20 October 2026. State population totals are the Census Bureau Vintage 2025 estimates [44], and the issue history of the same admissions series is from the Delphi Epidata API [45], retrieved on 5 November 2026. The data-processing code and analysis-window definitions of the original submission are in the public repository https://github.com/wangchi2068/reproduction-number-targets-surveillance (commit 2f5c4074a11cd5dbc8744ce4bf0b706c19171156). The analysis plan (analysis/analysisplan.md, with Amendment 1 appended to it), Amendment 2 (analysis/analysisplanamendment2.md), their checksum files (analysis/analysisplan.lock and analysis/analysisplanamendment2.lock), the combined result file analysis/results.json, code, data extracts and simulation settings for every reported analysis are distributed with this article in its experiment directory. Running bash code/runall.sh from the distributed experiment directory regenerates every reported estimate, table and figure from the stored inputs. No individual-level or restricted data were used.
