A Proofs

A.1 Count law and conditional information

The probability generating function of one negative binomial offspring count is [1+(Rt/k)(1−z)]−k. Conditional independence raises this function to the power n, and substituting z↦1−ρ+ρz for independent reporting gives [1+(ρRt/k)(1−z)]−nk, which proves Eq. (2); its derivatives give the stated moments.

For fixed, known (n,ρ,k) and R>0, the count likelihood has the score and Fisher information:

ℓ̇(R)=cR−(c+nk)ρk+ρR=ℐ(R)(R̂−R),ℐ(R)=mR+ρR2/k.(A.1)

By Eq. (A.1), Var(R̂∣R)=ℐ(R)−1. The support does not depend on R, so the regular one-parameter Cramér–Rao inequality applies to estimators unbiased for every R and gives the attained bound stated in Section 2.2 [24]. The bound therefore applies to estimators unbiased for every R with ρ and k known; biased estimators and unknown nuisance parameters require a separate analysis.

Proof of Proposition 1

Let et=R̂t−Rt. The error is conditionally centred, E(et∣Rt)=0, and its second moments are as follows:

E(et2)=ERt+ρERt2/km=Am,E[et(Rt−R¯)]=0.

Squaring Eq. (4) proves Eq. (3). Any estimator based on the same count and unbiased conditional on every Rt has expected conditional variance at least E[ℐ(Rt)−1]=A/m, and its process-mean risk adds the same vR. At fixed ρ, k and transmission law, [V(m)−V(2m)]/V(m)=1/[2(1+m/m×)] for vR>0. The comparison changes exposure n; it does not hold unchanged when the reporting probability changes. The shrinkage weight in Eq. (5) is Cov(Rt,R̂t)/Var(R̂t)=vR/V(m).

Proof of Corollary 1

Conditional on the path R1:T, the et are independent and centred, hence pairwise uncorrelated and orthogonal to every square-integrable function of the path. Thus the average of e1,…,eT has second moment A/(Tm), and Var(R̂¯T)=Var(R¯T)+A/(Tm). Under the stated stationary autocovariance, summing all covariance pairs gives T2Var(R¯T)=vRS(ϕ,T) with the first expression in Eq. (7), and the finite geometric sum yields the second [66]. Summing spatial covariance pairs in the same way gives Eq. (8), for any admissible correlation matrix.

Proof of Proposition 2 and Corollary 2

Write zt=pt/ρ and ut=Ct/m−ztRt. Conditional on (Rt,pt), ut has zero mean. Independence of pt and Rt, with Ezt=1 and Ezt2=1+τ2, gives:

E(ut2)=R¯+ρ(1+τ2)(R¯2+vR)/km=AHm.

The error R̂t−Rt=ut+(zt−1)Rt has uncorrelated terms, and the second has expected square τ2(R¯2+vR)=vH, which proves Eq. (11). Because E(R̂t−Rt∣Rt)=0, process-mean risk adds vR. Under the additional cross-period assumptions of Corollary 2, the errors are centred and independent given the transmission path after integrating out reporting, which gives Eq. (12).

For the identification statement, set U=(1+τ2)(R¯2+vR). The two moments of the scaled count are:

ER̂t=R¯,Var(R̂t)=U−R¯2+R¯+ρU/km.(A.4)

Whenever distinct admissible values of τ2 give vR=U/(1+τ2)−R¯2≥0, the moments in Eq. (A.4) coincide, and varying an exogenous m does not separate them. This proves nonidentification by these moments only; it does not assert equality of full count distributions.

For vR>0, the crossover scale with volatile reporting, m×,H=AH/(vR+vH), satisfies:

m×−m×,H=τ2(R¯2+vR)R¯(1+ρR¯/k)vR(vR+vH)≥0.(A.5)

Equality holds exactly when τ=0.

A.5 Observed denominator

Let Mt∼Bin(n,ρ) be independent of the offspring given n, and write Mt=m(1+ut), so that Eut=0 and Var(ut)=(1−ρ)/m. Then R̃t=R̂t/(1+ut). To first order in ut and R̂t−Rt, the error is approximately:

R̃t−Rt≈(R̂t−Rt)−Rtut.

Given (n,Rt), ut is independent of R̂t−Rt and centred, so the cross term vanishes and E[(R̃t−Rt)2]≈A/m+(1−ρ)E(Rt2)/m, which is Eq. (9). The Monte Carlo check in Table 3 draws Rt from a gamma law with the stated moments and would discard draws with Mt=0, none of which occurred at the scales shown. The approximation neglects the convexity of 1/(1+ut), which inflates the error when m is small; at m=10 the Monte Carlo error is 1.64 times the delta value.

A.6 Reporting shocks in the ratio statistic

Let the count of week t in a state be reported with probability ρzt, where the shocks zt are independent between weeks with logzt∼N(−s2/2,s2). To first order, the statistic in Eq. (14) satisfies logRA,t≈const+κ(g)loggt with κ(g)=(gμ/7)/[1+θlog(g)/7], because αθ=gμ. The shocks enter the observed growth factor as loggt=loggttr+ηt, with ηt=logzt+1−logzt and gttr the growth factor without shocks. Hence Var(ηt)=2s2, and the relative variance that the shocks add to the ratio statistic is:

ṽH≈2κ2s2.(A.7)

This component does not scale with count and therefore enters the intercept a. A reporting level that is constant over consecutive weeks of a state (zt+1=zt) gives ηt=0 and cancels. Consecutive rows share one shock with opposite signs, so Cov(ηt,ηt+1)=−s2 and their correlation is −1/2. The affine fit uses squared deviations, and for jointly Gaussian terms a correlation of −1/2 becomes a correlation of +1/4 between their squares. Resampling single weeks does not preserve this serial dependence, so interval coverage was checked directly. Under the audit generators S6 and S8 (Appendix C), which contain such shocks, the pigeonhole bootstrap intervals for a, b and b/a covered the Monte Carlo means of their estimators in at least 99.5% of 400 panels (Table 21). Under the fresh-draw generators with such shocks its standard deviation for a exceeded the Monte Carlo value by a factor of 1.55–1.67 (Table S13). For the realised mean over T consecutive rows of one state the mean of the shock terms telescopes to (logzT+1−logz1)/T, so their contribution to the error of the realised mean falls as T−2 rather than T−1. With κ near 0.5 for the primary interval and s=0.122 as in generator S6, Eq. (A.7) gives a shock component of about half the observed intercept.

B Extensions

B.1 Forecasting and shrinkage

Under fixed, known reporting and the stationary covariance of Corollary 1, with the counting error at t centred given the transmission path, the best forecast of Rt+1 of the form R¯+λ(R̂t−R¯) has the weight and risk:

λ*=ϕvRvR+A/m=ϕγ(m),MSElin=vR−ϕ2vR2vR+A/m.(B.1)

This follows from Cov(R̂t,Rt+1)=ϕvR. The forecast weight in Eq. (B.1) is the shrinkage weight discounted by persistence, and its limit risk is (1−ϕ2)vR. For the process mean, shrinking R̂t towards a fixed benchmark μ0 with oracle weight V(m)/[V(m)+(μ0−R¯)2] can give risk below vR; this lies outside the conditionally unbiased class of Proposition 1, and estimating the weight requires its own risk analysis.

B.2 Allocation between periods, cases and coverage

Proposition 3 (Budget allocation between periods and cases). Under H1–H4, independent, identically distributed transmission periods, conditionally independent counts, fixed ρ and linear costs, let the budget be ℬ=T(c0+c1m) with c0,c1>0, and treat T≥1 and m>0 as continuous. If vR>0 and ℬ>c0, process-mean risk (c0+c1m)(vR+A/m)/ℬ is strictly convex in m and is minimised at:

m*=min{(c0m×/c1)1/2,(ℬ−c0)/c1}.(B.2)

The optimum in Eq. (B.2) has the form of cluster-size allocation in survey sampling and multilevel design [12, 67]: cases per period should grow only with the square root of m× and of the relative cost of a period. Integer designs compare the risk over feasible integer T with nT=⌊(ℬ/T−c0)/(c1ρ)⌋. Under temporal dependence the variance term becomes vRS(ϕ,T)/T2 and no closed-form optimum follows.

Corollary 3 (Coverage against completeness). Under H2–H5, let pt be the participating fraction of ν independent reporting units, each participating with probability ρ, so that τ2=(1−ρ)/(ρν). A proportional increase in completeness ρ reduces single-period process-mean risk more than the same proportional increase in exposure n exactly when m>ρ2(ν−1)/k.

Write the single-period risk as vR+vH+AH/m with vH=τ2Q, Q=R¯2+vR and m=ρn, and differentiate with respect to logρ and logn. The difference of the two derivatives is:

∂risk∂logρ−∂risk∂logn=−Qkn[kn+ρρν−1].

Because Q/(kn)>0, the difference is negative, and a proportional increase in ρ lowers the risk more than the same increase in n, exactly when kn+ρ>ρν, that is, when m>ρ2(ν−1)/k. The mechanism is assumed; observed facility participation alone does not imply it.

B.3 Number of seasons

Suppose S≥2 season effects are independent Gaussian with unknown mean and variance vS>0, and the count law given the effects does not depend on these parameters. Any estimator unbiased for vS then has relative standard error at least (2/(S−1))1/2. Observing the effects themselves gives at least as much information as the counts, and their sample variance is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator [11, 24]. With the four seasons analysed here the bound is (2/3)1/2=0.82, and additional admissions within the same seasons leave it unchanged. This bound concerns the precision with which the between-season variance component can be estimated; it is distinct from the power of a test of equal season intercepts, which depends on the size of the season differences relative to their standard errors and is reported in Section 5.9.

B.4 Thinning and the delta approximation

Binomial thinning provides a further check on the counting slope. Each unique state-week count is thinned once to Bin(C,q) for q∈{0.8,0.6,0.5,0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1}, and the thinned value is reused in every ratio that contains it. Recomputing the statistic and the fit, with the original Ct as regressor, gives the thinning response:

b(q)−b(1)≃c(1/q−1).(B.4)

Under the delta approximation c=bP whatever the original counting variation, because thinning adds known binomial variance. The ratio c/bP is therefore a check of that approximation and not of the data-generating process. Because the check of Eq. (B.4) rests on a delta approximation, its exact expectation was computed on the observed counts. For each retention probability q the expected increment of the inverse-count slope was evaluated by summing over the binomial law of every thinned count (Table S2; Fig. S1A). The exact increment rate is 0.467 at q=0.8, rises to 0.505 at q=0.3 and falls to 0.480 at q=0.2 and 0.384 at q=0.1. The least-squares rate over all q is 0.408, or 0.917 bP, against the Monte Carlo estimate 0.405 (0.366–0.441), or 0.909 (0.810–0.999) bP (Table S3).

The pooled rate is dominated by the smallest retention probability. The value q=0.1 carries 76% of the leverage in the least-squares rate (Fig. S1B), and without it the rate is 0.488, or 1.096 bP. At q=0.1 many thinned counts are small, and the delta approximation of the variance of a log thinned count fails there. At C=5 and q=0.1 the exact added variance of log(Bin(C,q)+0.5) is 0.21 of the delta value (Table S4; Fig. S1C). The positive-part truncation of the fitted mean never binds. The shortfall of the pooled rate below bP is therefore a property of the approximation at small thinned counts, not evidence about the data-generating process.

In the audit the ratio c/bP lies in 0.95–1.00 under S0, 0.96–1.04 under S4, 0.87–0.98 under S5, 0.83–0.93 under S3 and 0.81–0.92 under S6. The observed value lies outside the ranges of the generators with Poisson offspring (S0, S1, S2P and S4) and inside those with negative binomial offspring, but its confidence interval overlaps all of them. Because thinning adds known binomial variance whatever the original counting process, the check cannot separate offspring overdispersion from under-reporting.

C Known-truth simulation audit

C.1 Design

The audit is a simulation study with known truth, reported under the aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures structure of Morris et al. [68]. It asks what a, b, b/a and the thinning rate recover on the sampling design of the application. Synthetic counts were generated on the exact RA design: the 1,748 rows, 1,969 unique state-weeks and 210 state runs of the data. Each run is simulated as a whole with shared counts, so that one week’s count is the next week’s denominator. The expected count is carried forward by the true growth factors, and the geometric-mean observed growth g0=1.407 is used for transitions that are not scored. The simulated Ct serves as the count scale, the filter Ct≥5 is re-applied, and the estimand of each row is the transform (14) of its true growth factor.

Two alignment steps fix the level of the synthetic panels, and the quantities they fix are calibration targets rather than tests. Each run is level-anchored to the geometric mean of its observed counts, and one scale factor per generator, between 0.797 and 0.844, sets the Monte Carlo mean of the median retained count to the observed median of 45. In every generator with transmission heterogeneity, the amplitude of that heterogeneity is then set so that the Monte Carlo mean of the fitted intercept equals the observed a. The slope ratio b/bP, the crossover b/a, the thinning rate, the pooled-to-within-state slope ratio, the reduction of a under week centring and the score contrast between affine and power-law fits are not targeted and serve as tests. A generator passes a test when the observed point value lies inside its 2.5–97.5% Monte Carlo range. This decision rule and the week-centring test were fixed after the generators had first been compared with the data, and Table 20 applies them to every generator. The lower tail of the retained counts matches the data (10th percentiles 10–11 against 10), but the upper tail does not, since the generators’ 90th percentiles are 263–324 against 389 observed (Table 18). Post-stratifying retained rows to the observed deciles of the count moves intercept recovery by at most 3.2%.

Table 17 sets out the design. The generators span the mechanisms that the diagnostics are meant to separate, from independent Poisson counts (S0) to scale-dependent heterogeneity combined with state-week reporting shocks (S8). Generator S9, which carries half of the S8 transmission heterogeneity in a national calendar-week component, was added after the others had been compared with the data. All generators in this appendix keep one heterogeneity field fixed across replicates; the interval checks of the analysis plan (Section 5.10) redraw it in every replicate.

C.2 Results

Without reporting shocks the intercept tracks the relative variance of transmission. When transmission is constant (S0, S2 and S2P) the fitted intercept is essentially zero. With independent heterogeneity, the ratio of a to the true relative variance on the retained rows is 1.01 (Monte Carlo range 0.93–1.09) under S1 and 1.02 (0.91–1.13) under S3. With structured heterogeneity it is 1.12 (1.04–1.19) under S4 and 1.15 (1.06–1.27) under S5 (Table 18; Fig. 9C). With reporting shocks that are fixed across replicates the intercept approximates the sum of both components: under S6, a is 1.01 (0.87–1.14) times the total ṽR+ṽH and 2.02 (1.71–2.29) times ṽR alone. Scale-dependent heterogeneity biases the intercept in the other direction, to 0.68 (0.60–0.78) and 0.43 (0.37–0.50) of the true relative variance under S7a and S7b, because variation that shrinks with count is absorbed by the slope. Under S8 the two distortions combine, and a is 1.75 (1.47–2.04) times ṽR and 0.85 (0.72–0.99) times the total. When the shocks are redrawn in every replicate the intercept falls 6–22% short of the total (Section 5.6), so the near-equality under S6 does not carry over.

The counting slope does not identify the mechanism. The ratio b/bP is 0.93 (0.85–1.01) under S0, 0.80 (0.73–0.86) under S2P and 1.23 (1.13–1.32) under S2 (Table 19; Fig. 9A). The step from S0 to S2P reflects the branching structure of denominator noise, and the step from S2P to S2 reflects offspring overdispersion. Transmission heterogeneity moves the ratio in both directions, from 0.73 under S4 to 2.25 under S7b. Among generators with heterogeneity the crossover count ranges from 22.2 (17.0–27.7) under S4 to 42.1 (30.8–58.2) under S8, so it does not discriminate between mechanisms either.

The curve shape separates generators more sharply. Generators with heterogeneity that does not depend on count give in-sample score differences of 0.012 (S1) to 0.024 (S5) in favour of the affine form, whereas the observed difference is −0.0014, a value reached by at most 0.3% of their panels (Fig. 9D). Under S8 the observed contrast lies at the 0.069 quantile, and the observed crossover and slope ratio lie inside the S8 ranges, but S8 does not reproduce the pooled-to-within slope ratio or the week-centring reduction. S9 raises the week-centring reduction to 19.1% (12.5–25.9), still below the observed value. No generator passes every test, and S8 and S9 pass four of six (Table 20). The held-out version of the contrast points the same way (Table S9). The audited generators therefore bracket the data on most summaries without reproducing all of them. An earlier exploratory grid over the transmission share and the scale dependence of the heterogeneity, not part of the analysis plan, gave implied transmission relative standard deviations of 5.1–20.5% across its 25 cells with heterogeneity; it is superseded by the grid of Table 9.

C.3 Interval calibration

The state-by-week pigeonhole bootstrap is conservative on this design (Table 21). Across S1, S6, S8 and S9, its intervals for a, b and b/a covered the Monte Carlo mean of the corresponding estimator in at least 99.5% of panels, against a nominal 95%, and the mean bootstrap standard deviation exceeded the Monte Carlo value by a factor of 1.6–2.5. Under the fresh-draw generators, which redraw the heterogeneity field in every panel, the ratio for a was 1.55–1.78 (range over panels 1.19–2.22), and the percentile intervals covered the mean of â in 0.99–1.00 of panels (Table S13). Every ratio exceeds 1, so the pigeonhole intervals are conservative under both kinds of generator, in line with the known overestimation of variance by the pigeonhole bootstrap in crossed designs [53, 69]. For the mean of a homoscedastic crossed random-effects design, the standard-deviation ratio is at most the square root of 3, about 1.73 [53]. The largest ratio, 1.78 under FD-S1, lies slightly above this bound. The Monte Carlo standard deviation comes from 200 panels and carries a relative standard error of about 5%, so the excess of 3% is within Monte Carlo error. The bound also applies only approximately to â, a weighted estimator with heteroscedastic rows. The fixed-field ratios of up to 2.5 further reflect the Monte Carlo variation that fixed fields understate. The two-way sandwich covered the mean of â in 0.993, 0.925, 0.925 and 0.983 of panels under S1, S6, S8 and S9. Under these fixed-field generators the ratio of the observed sandwich standard error of a to the Monte Carlo standard deviation was 1.7–2.9, which motivated the redrawn generators of Section 5.10. The Wald statistic for equal season intercepts was liberal at the χ32 critical value under the fixed-field generators, rejecting a true null in 0.195 of S6 panels and 0.217 of S8 panels, which is why asymptotic and generator-based references are not used as primary calibrations for the season test.

D Supplementary tables and figures

Tables S1–S9 give the slope references, the thinning check, the participation adjustment, the within-state slopes, the off-season reporting descriptors and the held-out comparison of curve shapes cited in the main text. Tables S10–S14 give the decile fits, the state-structured generators, the clamp sensitivity of the wild bootstrap, the pigeonhole bootstrap under fresh-draw generators and the type of every interval quoted in the text. Table S5 also reports the growth-factor statistic G of the original analysis, which the revised analysis does not use, and season-specific fits with separate slopes, which differ from the common-slope season intercepts of Table 15.

Data-informed generator design; no inferential result uses these generators.
